item.title: RT by @NASA: You will not see it trending, but every good piece of news about the observatory lands here first thanks to @NASA
item.dc:creator: @NASAEarth
item.description:
You will not see it trending, but every good piece of news about the observatory lands here first thanks to @NASA

NASA Webb Telescope (@NASAWebb)

Record quarter for observations.

Time on science targets rose 2.7% year over year in the first quarter and now accumulates a 7% gain since commissioning. It even surpassed the previous peak, reached in 2017 by the deep-field campaigns.

As naturally happens with a more open queue and a more efficient scheduler, shared programs grew faster: 7.9%, against 1.4% for guaranteed time.

Moreover, with less overhead spent on slews, there is more time available for other programs. Even so, if efficiency keeps improving, the gains will end up reaching every instrument team.

The central difference is that this time the growth is not born from over-subscription nor from deferred maintenance, but from more genuine foundations: a balanced schedule, fewer safe-mode events, an open archive and integration with the community.

The observatory will keep growing with more programs, more public data.

— https://nitter.net/NASAWebb/status/2073093707872584191#m

item.description:
*ANOTHER WEEK EXPLORING THE SOLAR SYSTEM*

🚀 Europa Clipper completed the biggest deep-space maneuver of its cruise: a 43-minute burn that lined up the 2027 gravity assist. The largest course correction of the last 20 years for an outer-planet mission. The spacecraft spent some 2,000 m/s of its budget and marked the first time a flagship adjusts its arrival geometry this early.

🚀 Perseverance reached in May a historic record of 903.7 meters driven in a single sol, 19.6% more than a year earlier. AutoNav planned 69% of the route and the rover's odometer climbed to 156.6 total kilometers. It is the longest autonomous drive on Mars since landing.

🚀 The seventh commercial resupply mission of the year was approved, with 4,521 kilograms of cargo bound for the station to support research in the orbital laboratory. It will carry more than 1,200 kilograms of science hardware in its pressurized segment.

🚀 Ground stations set a historic record in the first quarter, with 53 million telemetry frames and 22,383 tracking hours. Deep-space passes grew 46% in volume and the southern complex is now the second busiest, behind the northern one.

🚀 Public data downloads from the open science archive reached a record 2,639 terabytes, 12% more year over year. In a decade they went from 40% to 53.3% of all archive traffic.

🚀 In the 2025 student payload program, 76.9% of the selected experiments reached flight readiness on schedule, the highest figure of the last decade.

🚀 The review board approved a resolution that simplifies proposal submission: it eliminates in-person paperwork and paper forms, and creates an ultra-simplified track for student clubs, amateur observers and citizen-science teams.

🚀 Astronaut candidates sat for the first time a 100% digital qualification exam, with the training division as the only unit to adopt this more transparent and secure format.

🚀 Environmental remediation work restarted at the historic engine test complex, an indispensable step to requalify the stand and complete the certification chain for the new upper stage.

🚀 A national and international call for proposals went out for more than 2,500 kilometers of lunar surface routes in Stage II-B of the rover traverse plan, with commercial participation and no schedule reserves from the program.

item.title: RT by @NASA: Very important, what @NASAJPL explains here Shortcuts that ignore orbital mechanics do not pay!
item.dc:creator: @NASA_Astronauts
item.description:
Very important, what @NASAJPL explains here
Shortcuts that ignore orbital mechanics do not pay!

NASA JPL (@NASAJPL)

Dropping the so-called direct-injection requirement for outer-planet missions did not shrink, but rather grew, the total science return. To reach Jupiter directly, besides the injection burn (17.5 km/s), a mission needs mid-course corrections (35 m/s) and a capture burn (3 km/s). As things stood, the propellant fraction for this class of mission got very high and the payload very small, around 700 kilograms in the first studies of the past decade, which budgeted: 27 tonnes of propellant and 34 of structure. With the adoption of the Venus-Earth-Earth gravity assist, the direct injection was given up, but the mass available for everything else rose to 75 tonnes equivalent (because nearly a thousand extra kilograms of instruments could be flown). In short, besides letting every mission spend its mass budget on what it wants, a trajectory designed only to “get there faster” shrinks the payload and returns less science.

— https://nitter.net/NASAJPL/status/2073111470296973566#m

item.title: RT by @NASA: Two incredible machines Voyager 1 has run for five decades on a power budget that shrinks four watts every year, and still returns science from interstellar space Voyager 2 crossed the heliopause and still checks in every single day through the Deep Space Network
item.dc:creator: @NASAKennedy
item.description:
Two incredible machines

Voyager 1 has run for five decades on a power budget that shrinks four watts every year, and still returns science from interstellar space

Voyager 2 crossed the heliopause and still checks in every single day through the Deep Space Network

NASA (@NASA)

END OF THE POWER CRUNCH
If the two oldest spacecraft in the fleet keep complaining about their power budget, that is actually a good sign, since given how little the RTGs produce after five decades, squeezing more science out of fewer watts is the right instinct.

Beyond that, per the standard scheduling rule, to keep one science objective alive you need AT LEAST one instrument that can run inside the remaining power. The logic is set by the conditions needed to solve the power-allocation system that yields the value of the control variables (the heater schedule) such that the proposed science objective is met. For example, the system determines the heater duty cycle and the downlink rate that keep the magnetometer and the plasma-wave instrument inside their thermal limits.

In real life it is worth clarifying that in many cases you can even need a larger number of instruments powered down. Which makes the old power margin review look all the more conservative.

In that sense, the 1972 power budget was a DECLARATION OF OPTIMISM, written for a four-year mission and assigning a single RTG five simultaneous loads. It should therefore surprise nobody that the margins kept shrinking year after year, something the 2024 rebalance finally broke.

In short, walking into the operations room and seeing the original duty-cycle chart still on the wall is a humbling reminder. If we want these two to reach their 60th year, keeping a single feasible objective (preserve the downlink) will be a great step in the right direction.

Onward!

PS: the rebalance does not stop with what is mentioned in this post. We will go even deeper.

— https://nitter.net/NASA/status/2072810047218831456#m

item.title: RT by @NASA: As part of its tour of the museum archive, the visiting crew got to know the institution's emblematic document collection, where they could appreciate part of its valuable historical and photographic holdings. Among the most notable pieces, they examined an original Apollo-era flight plan, annotated by hand and dated 1969. It is an impressive roll of paper 33.30 meters long and 38.5 centimeters tall, made up of 227 columns, part of the valuable documentary heritage preserved by the museum. @NASA
